title: From Malaria to Kidney Injury: Erythrogram Profiles Across the Acute Kidney Injury– Acute Kidney Disease Spectrum
content: Background: Malaria-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and serious complication among hospitalized patients, but the relationship between erythrogram abnormalities and the spectrum of kidney dysfunction, including acute kidney disease (AKD), remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated erythrogram profiles across the AKI–AKD spectrum among patients hospitalized with malaria in Luanda, Angola. Methods: A hospital-based observational study was conducted among 400 patients hospitalized with malaria at Josina Machel Hospital–Maria Pia, between March and August 2023, in Luanda, Angola. Hemoglobin (Hb), red blood cell (RBC) count, hematocrit (Hct), mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and red cell distribution width (RDW) were assessed. Kidney involvement was initially classified as AKI or no AKI and subsequently categorized across the spectrum of no AKI, AKI1, AKI2, and AKD. Results: A total of 153 (38.2%) patients developed AKI. Patients with AKI had higher serum creatinine and uric acid concentrations, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate, and higher parasite density than those without AKI. Although MCV (p=0.045), MCH (p=0.001), and MCHC (p=0.003) distributions differed significantly between participants with and without AKI, these associations were attenuated after adjustment. Low hemoglobin was observed in 59.6% of patients with AKD compared with 36.8% of those without AKI, while low MCV was observed in 76.9% and 46.3%, respectively (p<0.05). After multivariable analysis, AKD remained associated with abnormalities in hemoglobin (AOR: 2.53; 95% CI: 1.37-4.66) and MCV (AOR: 4.63; 95% CI: 2.22-9.69), indicating a pattern of anemia and microcytosis among patients with persistent renal dysfunction. Conclusions: Patients with AKD demonstrated a distinct hematological phenotype characterized predominantly by anemia and microcytosis. These findings suggest that persistent kidney dysfunction may be associated with disturbances in erythropoiesis and red-cell morphology than acute kidney injury alone.
